clinicalScope: Acute pancreatitis in adults presenting to low‑resource hospitals in East Africa and similar settings
title: Acute Pancreatitis
subject: Medicine
summary: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas that can cause severe abdominal pain and systemic illness. In East African hospitals the most common triggers are gallstones, alcohol and infections, and limited diagnostics shape management.

sections.p: Acute pancreatitis (AP) is an abrupt inflammatory response of the pancreas that may extend to peripancreatic tissues and distant organs.
b: Incidence in sub‑Saharan Africa is estimated at 30–50 per 100 000, lower than high‑income regions but likely under‑reported.
Male predominance (≈2:1) reflecting higher alcohol use.
Peak age 30–60 years, coinciding with gallstone disease and alcohol consumption patterns.
Mortality ranges from 5 % (mild) to >30 % (severe necrotizing) when intensive care is unavailable.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Identify the trigger early because specific measures (e.g., stone removal) improve outcome.
b: Gallstones (biliary obstruction) – most common overall and in women.
Alcohol excess (>40 g/day) – leading cause in men and in rural areas where cheap spirits are consumed.
Hypertriglyceridaemia (>1000 mg/dL) – increasingly seen with uncontrolled diabetes and HIV‑associated dyslipidaemia.
Infections (mumps, coxsackie, HIV, CMV) – relevant in tropical settings.
Post‑ERCP trauma – less frequent where endoscopy is limited.
Medications (azathioprine, valproate, tetracyclines) – consider recent drug changes.
Trauma (blunt abdominal injury) – common after road‑traffic accidents.

sections.p: Premature activation of pancreatic enzymes within acinar cells initiates autodigestion and a cascade of inflammation.
b: Alcohol and gallstones cause ductal obstruction → increased intraductal pressure.
Calcium overload and oxidative stress trigger trypsinogen → trypsin conversion.
Trypsin activates other enzymes, injuring acinar and endothelial cells.
Cytokine release (IL‑1, IL‑6, TNF‑α) leads to systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
Microvascular thrombosis and necrosis develop if perfusion falls.

sections.p: Classic presentation guides early recognition even when labs are unavailable.
b: Sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back, often described as “knife‑like”.
Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distension.
Tenderness with guarding; may have absent bowel sounds in severe cases.
Fever, tachycardia, and hypotension indicate systemic involvement.
Skin: Grey‑white (Grey‑Turner) or flank bruising (Cullen) if hemorrhagic.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and exam narrow the differential and reveal severity clues.
b: Ask about recent alcohol binge, gallstone history, lipid disorders, recent infections or procedures.
Enquire about medication changes, trauma, and HIV/TB status.
Examine for epigastric tenderness, guarding, and peritoneal signs.
Check for jaundice (suggests biliary obstruction) and signs of chronic liver disease.
Assess fluid status: capillary refill, skin turgor, orthostatic vitals.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic AP share abdominal pain but differ in management.
b: Biliary colic/cholecystitis – pain usually right‑upper quadrant, no enzyme rise.
Peptic ulcer perforation – sudden severe pain with free air on X‑ray.
Acute mesenteric ischemia – pain out of proportion, often in atrial fibrillation.
Septicemia from intra‑abdominal sources – systemic signs without pancreatic enzyme elevation.
Acute hepatitis – jaundice dominant, transaminases >10× ULN.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Prioritise tests that are available; interpret thresholds to confirm diagnosis and gauge severity.

t.b: Is pancreatic enzyme elevation present? ≥3 × upper limit confirms enzymatic criterion.
Is there leukocytosis or haemoconcentration? WBC > 12 × 10⁹/L or haematocrit > 44 % suggests severe disease.
Is hypocalcaemia present? <2.0 mmol/L indicates fat saponification and worse prognosis.
Is there gallstone disease or biliary dilation? Detects stones, ductal size, and fluid collections.
What is the extent of necrosis? CT Severity Index ≥ 7 predicts severe disease.

sections.p: Early severity assessment directs level of care and monitoring.
b: BISAP (within 24 h): score ≥ 3 predicts >15 % mortality.
Ranson criteria (admission + 48 h): ≥3 points = severe.
APACHE II ≥ 8 within 24 h correlates with high risk.
CT Severity Index ≥ 7 or necrosis > 30 % defines necrotizing pancreatitis.
In low‑resource settings, use BISAP plus clinical judgment.

sections.p: Local and systemic factors can worsen outcome or mask diagnosis.
b: Concurrent HIV infection – higher risk of opportunistic pancreatic infections.
Malaria or severe anemia – may blunt fever response.
Use of traditional herbal remedies – can cause toxin‑induced pancreatitis.
Co‑existing hepatitis B/C – liver dysfunction limits drug choices.
Pregnancy – gallstone disease more common; fetal monitoring required.

sections.p: Treat the cause, support organ function, and monitor for deterioration.
b: Initial resuscitation: 10–15 mL/kg crystalloid bolus; reassess MAP > 65 mmHg.
Analgesia: IV paracetamol ± opioid (e.g., morphine) – avoid NSAIDs if renal risk.
NPO (nil per os) for 24–48 h; start nasogastric suction only if vomiting or ileus.
Early ERCP within 24 h for biliary obstruction with cholangitis.
If hypertriglyceridaemia >1000 mg/dL, give insulin infusion and consider plasmapheresis where feasible.
Antibiotics only for proven infected necrosis or cholangitis; use broad‑spectrum (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole).
Monitor urine output, electrolytes, glucose; replace potassium and magnesium aggressively.
Escalate to ICU if BISAP ≥ 3, persistent hypotension, or respiratory failure.
Necrotizing pancreatitis – persistent pain, rising CRP, CT necrosis.
Infected pancreatic necrosis – fever, leukocytosis, gas on CT.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) – hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates.
Renal failure – oliguria, rising creatinine.
Hemorrhagic pancreatitis – drop in haemoglobin, retroperitoneal bleed on imaging.

sections.p: Tailor care for populations with unique risks.
b: Pregnant women – prioritize maternal stabilization; consider early delivery if gestation > 34 weeks and severe disease.
Children – gallstone disease rare; consider trauma or genetic causes; dosing of fluids adjusted to weight.
HIV‑positive patients – screen for CMV or Mycobacterium avium complex pancreatitis; avoid azathioprine.
Patients with sickle cell disease – higher risk of gallstones; ensure adequate hydration.
Mild AP resolves in 1–2 weeks; advise alcohol cessation and low‑fat diet.
Biliary AP: schedule elective cholecystectomy within 6 weeks to prevent recurrence.
Control triglycerides (<500 mg/dL) with fibrates and dietary measures.
Vaccinate against mumps and hepatitis B to lower infection‑related risk.
Arrange outpatient review at 2 weeks for pain, labs, and imaging if necrosis suspected.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
b: Serum amylase may be normal in hypertriglyceridaemia‑induced AP; rely on lipase or imaging.
Ultrasound can miss small stones; a negative study does not exclude biliary cause.
CRP rises slowly; early low CRP does not rule out severe disease.
Hypocalcaemia may be masked by calcium supplementation.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with hypotension or shock
Persistent vomiting with inability to tolerate fluids
New onset confusion, respiratory distress, or oliguria
Signs of peritonitis or abdominal rigidity

faq.q: Why is lipase preferred over amylase for diagnosis?
faq.a: Lipase is more specific to the pancreas and remains elevated longer, reducing false‑negative results.

faq.q: When is ERCP indicated in acute pancreatitis?
faq.a: When there is biliary obstruction with cholangitis or persistent jaundice, ideally within 24 hours.
Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended; they are reserved for proven infected necrosis.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect biliary rather than alcoholic pancreatitis? — Right‑upper‑quadrant pain, jaundice, ultrasound showing stones or dilated CBD.

A patient meets two of the three diagnostic criteria for AP but lipase is unavailable. How do you proceed? — Use amylase ≥3 × ULN plus characteristic pain and imaging if possible; start supportive care.

Explain why aggressive fluid resuscitation is critical in the first 24 h and the target endpoints. — Restores pancreatic microcirculation, prevents necrosis; aim MAP > 65 mmHg, urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/h.

How does hypertriglyceridaemia cause pancreatitis and what immediate therapy is indicated? — Triglycerides >1000 mg/dL are hydrolysed to free fatty acids causing acinar injury; start insulin infusion and consider plasmapheresis if available.
Interpret a BISAP score of 4 in a patient with AP. What is the next management step? — High risk of mortality (>15 %); admit to ICU, monitor organ failure, consider early imaging.
When is it safe to resume oral intake after acute pancreatitis? — Once pain subsides, nausea resolves, and the patient tolerates clear fluids without worsening; typically after 48 h of NPO.

Distinguish infected pancreatic necrosis from sterile necrosis on imaging and clinical grounds. — Gas within necrotic collection on CT, fever > 38.5 °C, leukocytosis; sterile necrosis lacks these features.
Why are NSAIDs avoided in the early phase of AP in low‑resource settings? — They can worsen renal perfusion and mask fever, increasing risk of renal failure.
Outline the rationale for early cholecystectomy after biliary AP. — Removes the source of obstruction, reduces recurrence, and is safe after inflammation subsides (usually within 6 weeks).

A pregnant woman at 30 weeks presents with AP. What modifications to management are required? — Maintain maternal fluid and pain control, avoid teratogenic drugs, consider early ERCP if obstructed, and involve obstetrics for fetal monitoring.
